cards.explanation: The answer is True. The text says it right up front: “Then the LORD raised up against Solomon an adversary, Hadad the Edomite, from the royal line of Edom.” Solomon is David's son and Israel's king, and Hadad is the first name on the trouble list. Royal line and all, he shows up like he's got an appointment. The LORD is the one who raised him up.

The answer is that he fled the country as a young boy. Verse 17 says Hadad was “…still just a young boy…” when he fled to Egypt, along with some Edomites who were servants of his father. Joab, the army's commander, had struck down every male in Edom, and yet Hadad is still around. A young boy on the run, and he's the one the LORD raises up against Solomon.

The answer is Egypt. Verse 17 says Hadad fled to Egypt along with some Edomites who were servants of his father. They didn't go straight there, either. They set out from Midian and went to Paran before reaching Pharaoh, king of Egypt (1 Kings 11:18).

The answer is a house and land and food. Verse 18 says Pharaoh “…gave Hadad a house and land and provided him with food.” Pharaoh is the king of Egypt. Hadad shows up with his men, and he gets a house, land and meals, which is a pretty strong welcome.

The answer is True. Verse 20 says Genubath was weaned in Pharaoh's palace by Queen Tahpenes herself, and that he “…lived there among the sons of Pharaoh.” Pharaoh is the king of Egypt, and Genubath is Hadad's son. So Hadad's boy lived right there among the royal kids.

The answer is that Hadad asks Pharaoh to let him return to his own country. Hadad hears that David, Israel's old king, has rested with his fathers and that Joab, the commander of the army, is dead. Then he says to Pharaoh, “Let me go, that I may return to my own country.” (1 Kings 11:21) Both of the men connected to Edom's tragedy are gone, and Hadad speaks up.

The answer is that Hadad lacked nothing but still wants to go. Pharaoh asks what he has lacked, and Hadad answers, “Nothing,” … “but please let me go.” (1 Kings 11:22) No complaint, no list, no explanation. The text leaves it there, and so do I.

The word is master. Rezon, son of Eliada, “…had fled from his master, Hadadezer king of Zobah…” (1 Kings 11:23) He gathered men to himself, and he ended up ruling over Aram with hostility toward Israel. So the second adversary starts out as a man on the run and ends up a ruler.

The answer is Damascus. After David killed the Zobaites, Rezon captained a band of raiders and “…went to Damascus, where they settled and gained control.” (1 Kings 11:24) A crew of raiders ended up running the town. That's how a runaway servant becomes a ruler over Aram (1 Kings 11:25).

The answer is False. Verse 25 says, “Rezon was Israel’s enemy throughout the days of Solomon, adding to the trouble caused by Hadad.” He ruled over Aram with hostility toward Israel. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, had a neighbor who stayed against him the whole time.

The answer is True. Verse 26 says, “Jeroboam was a servant of Solomon, but he rebelled against the king…” Jeroboam son of Nebat is an Ephraimite from Zeredah, and his mother is a widow named Zeruah. So this trouble comes from one of Solomon's own servants.

The answer is that Solomon puts him over the labor force of Joseph's house. Solomon, Israel's king, noticed that the young man was industrious, so “…he put him in charge of the whole labor force of the house of Joseph.” (1 Kings 11:28) Jeroboam is called a mighty man of valor, and his work got noticed. A big promotion, and the text goes on to call it Jeroboam's rebellion account.

The answer is that he tears it into twelve pieces. Ahijah the Shilonite, a prophet, “…took hold of the new cloak he was wearing, tore it into twelve pieces…” (1 Kings 11:30). It's just the two of them alone in the open field. A brand new cloak ripped to shreds, and it's a message from the LORD.

The word is tribes. Ahijah says the LORD will tear the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, “…and I will give you ten tribes.” (1 Kings 11:31) Ten pieces of cloak, ten tribes of Israel. The cloak was the picture, and the words explain it.

The answer is for the sake of David and Jerusalem. The LORD says, “But one tribe will remain for the sake of My servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel.” (1 Kings 11:32) David is Israel's earlier king, and Jerusalem is where the LORD chose to put His Name (1 Kings 11:36). Two reasons, friends, and the LORD names both Himself.

The reason the LORD gives is that they forsook Him to worship other gods. He says, “For they have forsaken Me to worship Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites.” (1 Kings 11:33) These are false gods of neighboring nations. The LORD is telling Jeroboam why the kingdom is being torn.

The answer is all the days of his life. The LORD says, “Nevertheless, I will not take the whole kingdom out of Solomon’s hand, because I have made him ruler all the days of his life for the sake of David My servant…” (1 Kings 11:34) Solomon, Israel's king, stays on the throne for his whole life. The tearing comes later.

The word is son. The LORD says, “But I will take ten tribes of the kingdom from the hand of his son and give them to you.” (1 Kings 11:35) Just before that, He said He would not take the whole kingdom out of Solomon's hand (1 Kings 11:34). The text names that son at the end of the passage (1 Kings 11:43).

The promise is that Jeroboam will be king over Israel. The LORD says, “But as for you, I will take you, and you shall reign over all that your heart desires, and you will be king over Israel.” (1 Kings 11:37) Jeroboam, once a servant of Solomon, hears he will be a king. I bet that field got very quiet.

The word is dynasty. The LORD says, “If you listen to all that I command you, walk in My ways, and do what is right in My sight in order to keep My statutes and commandments as My servant David did, then I will be with you. I will build you a lasting dynasty just as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you.” (1 Kings 11:38) The promise comes with an if. Listening comes first.
The answer is False. The LORD tells Jeroboam that He will humble David's descendants, but not forever (1 Kings 11:39). The humbling has an end. That's the LORD's own word on it, friends.

The answer is that he flees to Shishak king of Egypt. Verse 40 says, “Solomon therefore sought to kill Jeroboam. But Jeroboam arose and fled to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, where he remained until the death of Solomon.” Solomon is Israel's king, and Jeroboam is the servant he's after. Egypt is also where young Hadad fled earlier in this passage.

The answer is until Solomon dies. Jeroboam fled to Shishak king of Egypt, “…where he remained until the death of Solomon.” (1 Kings 11:40) He stays in Egypt until Solomon, Israel's king, is gone. The text sets his stay by Solomon's life, not by a number.

The answer is his son Rehoboam. Verse 43 says Solomon “…rested with his fathers and was buried in the city of his father David. And his son Rehoboam reigned in his place.” Solomon reigned forty years over all Israel (1 Kings 11:42). Rehoboam is the son the LORD's words pointed to (1 Kings 11:35).
